note: Each conclusion is set against checked quotations and numbers computed from NASA's tables. The verdict words are fixed and say only what the evidence allows. Summaries are our reading.

items.claim: In a BASS-II test, the flame goes out after the forced flow stops.
items.summary: True as observed, for a flame whose only air came from the fan. Five kinds of condition are documented under which stopping the flow does not end the burning, and one whole regime, partial gravity, has no data.
scope: free fall, on the space station
a solid sample in a small wind tunnel
oxygen between 13.6% and 22.2% at the start of the tests
forced flow as the flame's only air supply
pressure not recorded in the table

holds.quote: After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s
holds.source: Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) Summary Report, NASA TM, NTRS 20210011385

holds.text: BASS-II in PSI: 129 test rows, with oxygen at the start between 13.6% and 22.2%. The table records conditions and gas readings. It has no column saying whether each flame went out.

In 17 of the 129 BASS-II rows, at 14.8% to 20.9% oxygen, the flow columns themselves say in NASA's shorthand that the flame went out ('ext', 'out', 'extinguished'); 11 of them read 'down to ext'. In 7 rows they say the flame blew off; in 15 a display reads 0 and the row has no word on the flame.

items.claim: A material that passes the flammability test on Earth is safe to fly.
items.summary: NASA's documents report materials that burn in less oxygen in microgravity and in Martian gravity than in the standard test on Earth. The word 'safe' is not one the evidence can support.

holds.text: The standard upward-burning test is the worst case on Earth, where buoyant flow is strong. That is the reason it was long treated as a bound.

fails.title: Lower oxygen limits away from 1 g

items.quote: is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.quote: the 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen
items.source: Olson and Ferkul, Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test, NTRS 20130010991

items.quote: which some researchers believe is not conservative in low-g
items.source: NASA Glenn: Combustion Science

items.quote: This means that some things that are not flammable on Earth, may be flammable in potential habitats on the Moon and other places with reduced gravity
items.source: NASA Glenn: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)

untested.text: No row of any PSI combustion table was taken in lunar or Martian gravity.
8 rows lie near 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia and 11 near 34% at 8.2 psia; none of them is a solid material.

next.quote: If proven for more materials, this may indicate the need to include a factor of safety on 1g flammability limits
next.source: Olson and Ferkul, Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test, NTRS 20130010991

items.claim: NASA's microgravity combustion data cover the atmospheres planned for lunar and Martian habitats.
items.summary: They touch those atmospheres with a handful of gas and droplet rows. For solid materials and for partial gravity there is nothing to cover with.
scope: the 24 combustion records of PSI, as fetched for this site

holds.text: 746 of 887 test rows state both oxygen and pressure; 215 lie near the cabin air of the space station.
8 rows lie near 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia and 11 near 34% at 8.2 psia (near means within 0.03 in oxygen fraction and 15% in pressure).

items.text: Solid-material rows that state pressure: 0. The BASS-II and Saffire tables give oxygen only.
Rows near a suit atmosphere (pure oxygen at 4.3 psia): 0.
No row of any PSI combustion table was taken in lunar or Martian gravity.

untested.text: Whether the raw files of these records hold pressures that the experimental tables omit. The site reads the tables, a few summaries and one raw data file (the Saffire-III recording), not the other raw data.

next.quote: Conduct the first-ever observations and measurements of flame spread on the Moon
next.source: NASA Glenn: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)

items.claim: The flame-temperature model on this site agrees with NASA's own numbers.
items.summary: For the gas flames NASA tabulated, yes, to about two kelvin. It says nothing about solids, and for one record the agreement depends on reading NASA's column as a one-atmosphere value.
scope: gas flames of ethylene, propane, ethane and butane diluted with nitrogen
the 587 rows of four tables where NASA gives a number

holds.text: Model against NASA's Tad: 587 rows, mean difference 2.1 K, median 2.0 K, bias +0.5 K. Zst agrees to the fourth decimal.

fails.title: Where the agreement is weaker or conditional

items.text: The largest single difference is 18.8 K.
In PSI-159 the columns agree only when the model is run at one atmosphere. Run at the pressure each row states, the mean difference is 28.0 K and the largest 69.0 K.
73 rows were left out because NASA's cell or an input is not a number (ramp tests, spreadsheet errors).

untested.text: Solid materials, droplets, flame spread and extinction: NASA's tables carry no computed temperature for them, and an equilibrium temperature could not describe them anyway.
Diluents other than nitrogen. FLEX used carbon dioxide and helium; those rows have no Tad column to compare with.

next.text: A table from NASA with measured flame temperatures, or with Tad computed at the stated pressure, would test this directly.

items.claim: A smoke detector that works on Earth will work the same way in a spacecraft.
items.summary: NASA's documents say smoke itself is different without buoyancy, and that telling smoke from dust took a purpose-built detector.

holds.text: Detectors of both kinds have flown and have raised alarms; nothing here says they do not work.

In the same recording, with the cabin fan running, the detector's reading first exceeded its level of the minute before ignition 71.5 s after the igniter fired, was half-way to its peak after 161.5 s, and peaked after 341.5 s. The radiometers were back at baseline 356 s after ignition.

fails.title: A wire and a fire can read alike

items.text: Saffire-III, from the vehicle's own telemetry in PSI-100: the smoke detector's scatter reading peaked at 1.615 after a smoke wire was powered and at 1.805 while a sheet of fabric 94 cm long burned. It stayed above 0.81 for 10 s the first time and for 300 s the second. The file gives no units and no alarm level.

fails.title: The alarm can come after the gases

items.quote: Selecting 1 mg/m3 as a relatively tight alarm threshold, the FFD detector reached that threshold at 981 seconds. By this point, much of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
items.source: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, ICES-2024-365, NTRS 20240002981

items.text: In the two acrylic tests of Saffire VI, carbon monoxide at the far sensors rose by 308 and 320 ppm and carbon dioxide by 3.51 and 3.37 mmHg. NASA's limits in the same paper: 100 ppm of carbon monoxide for 24 hours, 425 ppm for one hour, 3 mmHg of carbon dioxide as a one-hour average. The highest temperature at the far sensors was 21 and 21 °C.

fails.title: The particles are not the same

items.quote: Fundamental research in microgravity highlighted the vastly different particulate size associated with flames in microgravity
items.source: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (NASA)

items.quote: can discriminate between combustion particles and extraneous matters such as dust
items.says: A detector first used in space shuttle orbiters
items.source: NASA Spinoff: Fire Detector (1978)

items.quote: Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
items.says: What a large fire changed most in a cargo vehicle
items.source: Urban et al., Preliminary Results from the Saffire VI Experiment, NTRS 20240002981 (abstract)

untested.text: No row of any PSI combustion table was taken in lunar or Martian gravity.
Smoke particle sizes in PSI come from two flight experiments (SAME and SAME-R) and a dust test (DAFT), all in free fall.

next.text: Particle-size data from a partial-gravity burn would show whether lunar smoke looks like Earth's, like the station's, or like neither.
